Statement of the problem: A 67-year-old man plans to build his retirement beach house on his two-hectare property in El Nido, a forested site with a natural beachfront and an existing jetty. Site features: The property gently slopes about 2% toward the west, where the beachfront and jetty are. The western edge was previously shaved down for the jetty. The eastern side is the highest point and connects directly to the access road (RROW). The surroundings are forested. The development consists of three detached roofed pods:
• POD 1, the Private Pod – Master Bedroom and Guest Bedroom; at the quietest, most stable part of the site near the upper east close to the RROW. The Master Bedroom has a balcony and a west-facing view deck with an unobstructed view of the water.
• POD 2, the Semi-Public Pod – Dining and Kitchen; the central hub and transition between private and public zones.
• POD 3, the Public/Leisure Pod – Infinity Pool, Pool Deck, Lanai, Bar, Outdoor Living Area and a dance area; at the lowest portion facing the beachfront, with direct access to the jetty.
A six-car garage is required, and service items such as the water pump and septic tank must be placed safely, accessibly and in compliance with environmental rules.

Design objectives: universal design for an elderly user (minimal level changes, ramps, wide doors, barrier-free circulation from the RROW down to the jetty); a clear privacy gradient – private zone at the upper east, semi-public at mid-site, public/leisure at the lower west; protect the owner from the grandchildren's noise; minimize glare while maximizing sunset views; use the slope to reduce cut and fill; efficient, accessible circulation between pods; landscaping for slope stabilization, privacy and a tropical resort feel; services that do not interfere with primary spaces.

PROJECT NO. 4 – A PROPOSED 300-BED TERTIARY (LEVEL-3) GENERAL HOSPITAL ON A GOVERNMENT-OWNED LOT

Statement of the problem: The LGU, with the Provincial Government and the DOH, will build a 300-bed Level-3 general hospital as a regional referral center, teaching and training hospital and disaster-response facility, offering emergency, outpatient, inpatient, diagnostic, surgical, specialty and critical care, plus residency training, research and simulation. It uses a podium-and-tower scheme: a Central Podium (public, diagnostic, treatment, procedural, administrative and academic functions) with Tower A (adult inpatient) and Tower B (specialty inpatient: pediatric, OB, isolation, step-down), allowing expansion without disrupting operations. It must comply with the NBC, the Fire Code, BP 344, DOH Level-3 licensing standards and local zoning.

Site: a 50,000 m² government-owned lot. The southern frontage (main road) is for public entry, OPD and visitors; the eastern barangay road is for service, logistics and loading; the western parcel is reserved for future expansion. Amihan winds come from the northeast; there is strong western afternoon sun; noise comes from traffic on the southern road. Flood risk is low to moderate. Public, emergency (dedicated ambulance route) and service traffic are separated. Building footprint about 17,500 m², organized around a Central Healing Garden between the podium and the two towers.

n: Without tactile cues, visually impaired people cannot find their way. BP 344 requires detectable wayfinding elements such as tactile paving. Source: BP 344 IRR (2024 amendment), tactile guide blocks.
scenario:
PROJECT NO. 4 – A PROPOSED 300-BED TERTIARY (LEVEL-3) GENERAL HOSPITAL ON A GOVERNMENT-OWNED LOT

Statement of the problem: The LGU, with the Provincial Government and the DOH, will build a 300-bed Level-3 general hospital as a regional referral center, teaching and training hospital and disaster-response facility, offering emergency, outpatient, inpatient, diagnostic, surgical, specialty and critical care, plus residency training, research and simulation. It uses a podium-and-tower scheme: a Central Podium (public, diagnostic, treatment, procedural, administrative and academic functions) with Tower A (adult inpatient) and Tower B (specialty inpatient: pediatric, OB, isolation, step-down), allowing expansion without disrupting operations. It must comply with the NBC, the Fire Code, BP 344, DOH Level-3 licensing standards and local zoning.

Site: a 50,000 m² government-owned lot. The southern frontage (main road) is for public entry, OPD and visitors; the eastern barangay road is for service, logistics and loading; the western parcel is reserved for future expansion. Amihan winds come from the northeast; there is strong western afternoon sun; noise comes from traffic on the southern road. Flood risk is low to moderate. Public, emergency (dedicated ambulance route) and service traffic are separated. Building footprint about 17,500 m², organized around a Central Healing Garden between the podium and the two towers.

Zoning and planning logic: public zone at the main entrance with direct access to OPD; emergency zone with separate ambulance access, direct access to surgery and ICU and immediate adjacency to imaging; critical care next to the surgical suite and close to imaging and ER; a sterile surgical zone with a direct relationship to CSSD; inpatient wards in the quietest part of the site, oriented north or east toward the healing garden; service and support on the east side with dirty traffic kept off sterile routes. Separate public, patient, bed, staff, service, clean, dirty and sterile circulation; two remote exits per floor, smoke-proof stairs, fire compartments, sprinklers, fire detection and a fire command center.

q: A hospital design proposes connecting the Laboratory sink to the same sanitary line as the public toilets. Which utility-planning principle is MOST likely compromised?

Segregation and proper treatment of laboratory wastewater before discharge
n: Laboratory wastewater carries chemicals and pathogens, so it must be segregated and treated before it joins the sanitary system. Source: DOH Health Care Waste Management Manual; National Plumbing Code of the Philippines (special wastes).
